newsitem.title: UK: LME must keep pace with technology - CEO.
newsitem.headline: LME must keep pace with technology - CEO.

text.p: The London Metal Exchange (LME) will be looking at technology-related matters with a view to further strengthening its position as the world's leading metal exchange, according to LME chief-executive David King.

"It is essential that the LME embraces technologically-driven opportunities in order to maintain its global pre-eminence," King said in a speech prepared for delivery to the Fourth International Derivatives Conference in London on Wednesday.
"We will also be considering other issues arising out of the ever-changing environment in which the LME operates," he said.

King gave an update on the LME's implementation of the recommendations made by UK regulator, the Securities and Investments Board, in the wake of huge losses made in the copper market by Japan's Sumitomo Corp due to unauthorised trading by its head trader.

The LME has already changed the structure of its Board, instituted daily stock reporting, which seems to be working well, and has recently turned its attention to its sub-committees, King said in a similar speech made recently at a conference in Seville, Spain.

"The SIB report of December 1996, which the LME requested, identified no significant systemic risks arising from the way the LME operates. The SIB concluded that the LME, and its trading systems, continue to enjoy the overwhelming support of LME users," King said.

He said, " Trading at the LME remains strong, overall trading volumes have increased since the 'Sumitomo affair', unlike the situation following the 'Tin Crisis' of 1985, and there has been no net loss of either clients of member."
The LME is the world's largest non-ferrous base metals market, turning over 47 million lots in 1996 and generating 250 million sterling of UK invisible earnings.
